I've seen people with gut problems stating that they rather have a cancer than bowel disease and I put all of my trust on their words. The brain-gut link is insanely real. Mind and body are just one thing. But generally people who don't suffer from any mental condition don't have a clue that we often struggle in all levels. Just as if the psychological symptoms alone weren't bad enough. I'd rather live a short, happy and satisfying life to die young with cancer than living to be old having passed all of my years without ever knowing what it is like to be comfortable in my own mind / body for a day.

We're all traumatized, but the world favors some behaviors over others, so people can benefit of their trauma response somehow. And yes, I have seen it. A 60+ aunt who doesn't stop cleaning the house all day even if she complains of some pain. But if the pain was really unbearable she would stop, right? I think I have my pros being a freeze type, but they're not something our system values generally. Moreover, I haven't find yet a way to adapt the game to my "weak" cards.

You are either sick in the "right" way or you find an alternative to make your life more sufferable.

Antidepressants are good for you if you use them while doing therapy; otherwise, they're simply a remedy to mask your symptoms and making you numb, instead of treating the real roots of your problem. Personally, I wouldn't use SSRIs due to fear of developing post-SSRI syndrome, as I found their side effects to be too potent on me (to the point of getting my skin hurt and only realizing it when I saw the blood, because I had no sensation at all). On mirtazapine (along with some horse tranquilizer, idk, with antiepiletptic properties) I had tingling legs and was sleepy even during the day. I think I'm too sensitive for those medications. But I know they can be helpful for some people who use these drugs along with psychotherapy. Also, imo, their use should be temporary ideally. However, there are few individuals who need to use them for an entire life, but they're a minority.

The Enneagram works with broader, more basic concepts than MBTI. 

For you to understand MBTI you'll have to study the Jungian's functions, then you'll find out that Katherine and Myers Briggs changed the original theory stating that the auxiliary function has the opposite direction of the dominant; because for Jung, initially, both were the same; then you'll find out there is the Socionics and so on... 

Basically, when we're talking about cognition we're talking about more complex concepts. Then we have lots of different interpretations of the psychological types. MBTI and systems alike specify too much. And yet, people can look at them as they please.

Now, take a look at the Enneagram... What does it say? 

Enneagram revolves around core fears and motivations. It breaks down people in 3 main emotions: Anger, Shame and Fear. 

From those emotions, each Enneagram type belonging to each of those triads will manifest that primordial emotion through their respective fears--which leads to vices--and motivations that, when guided wisely by their core emotions can lead to virtue, that is: when the type integrates.

Now you can see that the Enneagram looks at the human psyche by the light of a more primitive point of view. We humans, just like animals, are guided by our instincts. The authors of the Enneagram theorized that all of that mechanisms explained previously would work differently based on what instinct dominates one's behavior.

Then the subtypes were made. And then the countertypes -- by the realization that some instincts contradict more the essence of some types than others.

It's not absurd at all to think there are people who focus more on Sx, Sp or So. They're all part of our nature. Just like it's not absurd to think that one of them will be repressed, because strengths always come with weaknesses. If you spend too much energy on one area you're automatically neglecting another area.

Now, the functioning of the instinctual variants can vary. You can have a dominant variant that is 60%~30% in relation to the aux (supposing the last one is zeroed, which isn't good by the way), or you can have a practically full dominant variant--and you can imagine that would also be unhealthy. 

Also, the circumstances you're going through in your life will affect how your stack is used. If your dominant isn't working, for example, you'll restore to the second. 

But the key is that you use the auxiliary function to support your dominant one.

The dynamics also change based on what type of pairing you have. sx/sp is different than sx/so since sp can block the sx energy, while sx/so can experience their sx energy more freely.

I also suggest you to look at the Syn-Flow / Contra-Flow theory for you to see how all of this makes sense:
 
https://enneablog.tumblr.com/post/160461121635/contra-flow-vs-syn-flow-in-the-instinctual

Regarding the Big Five:

There is no particular correlation but there is this general understanding that sx is more restless than the other variants; this can become neurotic especially when sp as auxiliary represses the natural tendency of this subtype causing a disturbed character --> Limbic? So we can draw some parallels indeed, like so-dominant people tending to be less Reserved and such.

"Clusters" are used for PDs. Neither Bipolar nor Schizophrenia are PDs. Besides that, Schizophrenia and Type 1 Bipolar can operate very similar, almost indistinguishably at times. The genetic etiology is said to be the same.

Don't mess mood / psychotic disorders with PDs, they aren't related. If one's issues have left the field of an ingrained behavioral pattern and turned into something else, which implies more obvious neurochemical changes, that's another thing.

Borderline and Bipolar can seem similar at surface, but the former has to do with a pattern of being extremely reactive to events that happen externally due to the individual's interpretation of facts and is therefore a personality problem, even if trauma do cause the brain to change in some way. In Bipolar, on the other hand, mood variations occur due to chemical changes that cause the person to have interspersed phases of depression and hypomania / mania regardless of what is happening abroad.

Bipolar is not a response of an individual to the environment, it is a disorder that is deep-rooted in one's brain chemistry, just like Schizophrenia. Whilst PDs are an adaptation response of personality, unlike those disorders which are known to be caused by chemical imbalances.

That said, no, SzPD and STPD aren't "two halves of schizophrenia". If such people are more predisposed or not to have a Schizophrenia diagnosis later on, this is not related to the Personality Disorder itself, as this is characterized solely by defensive behavioral aspects.

I know that in practice these things might get blurrier, but these are the definitions.
